performers: Enrico Caruso, tenor; Salvatore Cottone, piano
intro: In “Vesti la giubba”, from Pagliacci, Canio, a husband in despair, tells himself to put on his clown’s costume because he still has a show to give. Caruso recorded the aria in Milan in 1902, with Salvatore Cottone at the piano.

sections.label: B · Canio’s aria with piano
sections.mNote: Canio sings of laughing while grieving.

sections.mNote: Voice and piano take the aria to its close.

cues.title: Piano accompaniment, Milan, 1902
cues.text: Salvatore Cottone played the whole accompaniment at the piano, and Caruso sang Canio’s part. They recorded it in Milan on 30 November 1902.
cues.evidence: The Discography of American Historical Recordings identifies Caruso, Cottone and the Milan session of 30 November 1902. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/1000003400

cues.title: Act I, final scene
cues.text: Canio has caught his wife Nedda with another man. Peppe tells him to get dressed, because the audience is coming. Alone beside the little theatre, Canio must play the clown in spite of his own humiliation.
cues.evidence: Leoncavallo, Pagliacci (1892), Act I, final scene; libretto, Teatro Regio Torino, pp. 10–12. https://www.teatroregio.torino.it/sites/default/files/uploads/inline-files/20210807%20-%20Pagliacci%20-%20Libretto.pdf

cues.title: Text of “Vesti la giubba”
cues.text: The aria’s words are commands that Canio gives himself. He tells himself to put on the costume, powder his face and turn his sobs into a funny face. He orders himself to laugh at his broken love, because the paying public expects a comedy.
cues.evidence: Leoncavallo’s Italian text for Canio in Pagliacci, Act I, “Vesti la giubba” through “Ridi, Pagliaccio”. The note describes the aria’s text as a whole. https://www.opera-arias.com/leoncavallo/pagliacci/vesti-la-giubba/
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.
